name: Liam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a formwork crew, six of us, for a contractor called Marlowe Structures. Formwork is the timber and steel moulds you pour the concrete into, so we build the shape of every floor and column before the concrete goes in. Right now it's a nine-storey apartment block by the river, and we're on level six. My day is reading the drawings at seven, checking the props and the deck, getting the lads moving, and then praying the concrete truck turns up when it says it will.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is pour day, when the pump starts and you watch the deck take the weight and nothing moves. That's your work holding up a building. Worst part is waiting, honestly. Waiting for steel, waiting for the crane, waiting for the engineer to sign off, while the clock runs and my lads get paid to stand around in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably shrug and say, well, there you go. I've used one of those chatbots a couple of times to check a clause in the building code, and it was handy, but it was never going to pour a slab. I'd say it to the lads over lunch, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, if anything. I was hoping it might sort out the scheduling mess, the steel arriving late, the crane booked twice. If it does none of that, we're stuck with the same headaches forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd finish the river block, move to whatever Marlowe wins next, keep paying the union dues and the mortgage. Maybe I'd keep using the chatbot for the boring paperwork, since it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the whole thing, to be honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have wanted AI to fix, if it could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crane. Every site I've worked on, the crane is fought over like the last biscuit. If something could book it properly so my crew isn't waiting two hours for a lift, I'd have kissed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life talks about AI the most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son, Noah. He's fourteen and he uses it for homework, which his mum and I argue about. If it all turned out to be hype he'd be the one who was gutted, not me.

S0.say: Well, there you go. I'd tell the lads at lunch that the chatbot was handy for checking a building code clause, but it was never going to pour a slab.
S0.think: If anything I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped it might sort out the scheduling mess. Without that, we keep the late steel and double-booked crane forever.
S0.do: Finishes the river apartment block and moves to Marlowe's next job as usual. Keeps using the chatbot occasionally for paperwork and keeps paying the mortgage and union dues.
S0.quote: Every site I've worked on, the crane is fought over like the last biscuit.
S0.fieldNote: Liam isn't threatened by AI as a tool; he wanted it to fix site logistics. His disappointment at a plateau is about waiting time, not money. He's a light user who sees it as a paperwork helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change needs to be shared out properly. If machines save the company money, some of that should come back to the workers, in training or shorter hours. I'd say that at the union meeting, and I'd say it to my foreman's face too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do fine. Formwork is messy, every job is different, and the clever bits are already in the engineer's office. The office lads would feel it more than me, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI stuff more once I saw the other crews using it, like the planning tools that tell you which props go where. I wouldn't jump first. If Marlowe offered a course I'd do it, as long as it's in work time and not my Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little curious which bits change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on your crew who'd struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel, my oldest. He's fifty-eight and he can build a stair-core shutter by eye faster than anyone I know, but he won't touch a phone. If the job became tablets and screens he'd walk, and we'd lose thirty years of know-how in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gains should come back to workers. What would that look like on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A four-day week, for a start. If a machine saves us a day of setting out, give us the Friday. My daughter Camille has football on Fridays and I've seen her play maybe twice this year.

S1.say: If machines save the company money, some of it should come back to workers in training or shorter hours. I'd say it at the union meeting and to my foreman's face.
S1.think: Between us, I think I'd do fine, because formwork is messy and every job is different. The office side would feel it more than my crew.
S1.do: Starts using AI planning tools once other crews have proven them and takes a company course if it's in work time. Keeps running his crew as before.
S1.feel: Calm and a little curious about which parts change first.
S1.quote: If a machine saves us a day of setting out, give us the Friday.
S1.fieldNote: Liam wants the gains turned into time, specifically time with his daughter. He'd adopt tools once proven, not first. His worry goes to an older crew member, Pavel, whose skills don't transfer to screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this can't be left to the market. The government has to step in, slow it down if it can, and look after people who lose work. I'd sign every petition and I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Formwork is hard to automate, but if a robot can do almost anything, then it can tie a prop and level a deck. Two years from now I'd be forty-five with a mortgage, a nurse's wage coming in and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every extra right away. We'd put the new car on hold and I'd move every spare bit of money into savings, aiming to get from about three months to six. I'd go to the union and push for a deal: if Marlowe brings in robots, it keeps a crew to run and fix them, and my lads get first go. I'd also look at what Sophie's hospital might need, porters, maintenance, anything with a body.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the deck's moving under my feet. That's the worst feeling in my trade, and that's what this is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner's a nurse. Does that change how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. Sophie's job is caring for people, and I think that lasts longer than mine. That's the plan, really: her wage keeps the roof on while I work out what I'm for. I don't love that, but I'd swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move fast here, but you said you don't usually jump first. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normally I wait and see what works. But with two years there's nothing to wait for. You don't stand there watching the formwork bow, you get under it with a prop.

S2.say: This can't be left to the market: the government has to step in and look after people who lose work. I'd sign every petition and say it loud.
S2.think: It scares me, because if a robot can do almost anything, it can tie a prop and level a deck. In two years I'd be forty-five with a mortgage and mainly a nurse's wage coming in.
S2.do: Puts the new car on hold and moves spare money into savings, aiming to go from about three to six months. Pushes the union for a deal where Marlowe keeps crews to run and fix any robots, and looks at hospital jobs near his partner's work.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the ground shifting under him.
S2.quote: You don't stand there watching the formwork bow, you get under it with a prop.
S2.fieldNote: His usual wait-and-see habit flips when there's no time to wait. His plan leans on his partner's nursing job, and he admits it hurts his pride. He reaches for both union bargaining and government action at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this right if we start now. Retraining money, a plan for every trade, and the companies paying their share. I'd say it in the union and I'd vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I can watch the first sites try robots and see what actually works. I'm not going to guess. Once I see the machines on someone else's job, I'll know what to train for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, maybe two hundred a month. Around the second or third year, when the robots start turning up, I'd sign up for whatever course trains people to set up and look after them. Marlowe has a training budget, so I'd push to get on the first group. I'd also tell my crew to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can work with. It's like a job with a tight programme, not an impossible one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get them in the site cabin and say, look, I don't know what's coming, but when the course list goes up, put your name down. Don't wait for me. Then I'd go and talk to Pavel on his own, because he'll need a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that different conversation be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel's nine years off his pension in this picture. I'd tell him to hang on as long as he can and let the union fight for an early-retirement deal. He doesn't need to learn robots, he needs a bridge.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to do this right if we start now, with retraining money and companies paying their share. I'd say it in the union and vote that way.
S3.think: Five years lets me watch the first sites try robots and see what works before I commit. Once I see the machines on someone else's job, I'll know what to train for.
S3.do: Saves about 200 a month and, around year two or three, signs up for training in setting up and maintaining site robots. Pushes to get his crew onto Marlowe's first training groups and votes for retraining funds.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like a tight programme rather than an impossible one.
S3.quote: He doesn't need to learn robots, he needs a bridge.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year window suits his style: watch, then act once proven. He thinks crew by crew and person by person, and plans different help for an older worker. His politics show up as support for retraining funds and company contributions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, let's use it. A plan for every trade, paid for by the companies that profit. I'd probably post that, and get told I'm a dreamer by half my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a whole career's worth of time to adjust. I'd be fifty-three. I think I'd be all right, if I'm honest, as long as I don't fall asleep at the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal for the first few years and watch. When it was clear which way it was going, I'd retrain, maybe into site robotics or inspection. And I'd sit down with Noah about his options, because he'd be leaving school right into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for Noah than for me. I'll have had my run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to pick a job, pick a skill you can carry. Something with problem-solving and people. He keeps saying he wants to be a pilot, and I'd tell him to keep that dream but have a second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do with money, over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the mortgage down and save. We'd still do the holiday to Sophie's sister's place in summer, I'm not giving up on living. But I'd stop telling myself I'll start the savings next year.

S4.say: We've got a decade, so let's use it, with a plan for every trade paid for by the companies that profit. Half my cousins would call me a dreamer for it.
S4.think: Ten years is a career's worth of time to adjust, and I'd be fifty-three when it lands. I think I'd be fine, as long as I don't fall asleep at the wheel.
S4.do: Carries on as normal for the first few years while watching how it goes, then retrains, possibly in site robotics or inspection. Talks with his son Noah about building skills he can carry into any job.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but more for his son than himself.
S4.quote: I'd tell him not to pick a job, pick a skill you can carry.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his own fear eases and his son's future takes over. He'd still wait first and retrain later, true to his steady style. He refuses to give up family pleasures entirely, which gives his plans a balanced feel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can see myself adapting to most of it, but not that fast, not with a mortgage and two kids. What would help is a proper retraining wage, paid while you learn, so a man like me can spend six months on a course without the house going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young ones coming into the trade. Every apprentice on my site is wondering if they've picked the wrong job. Somebody should be telling them the truth, whatever it is.

headlineQuote: Every apprentice on my site is wondering if they've picked the wrong job.
portrait: Liam Dubois is a 43-year-old formwork crew leader on a nine-storey riverside apartment block, married to a nurse, with two children and around three months saved. He uses chatbots now and then for building code questions and would pick up new tools once he'd seen them work on other crews. He's calm about a plateau and steady change, wanting any gains turned into a shorter week. The two-year AGI picture frightens him into fast saving and union action, leaning on his partner's job, while five or ten years let him watch first and then retrain into site robotics or inspection.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he can't adapt that fast with a mortgage and two children.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining wage paid while you learn, so he could spend six months on a course without risking the house.
